podcast.title: Randy Bachman's Mormon Conversion and Band Tension (1966)
podcast.body: Randy Bachman's conversion to Mormonism in 1966 created significant tension within The Guess Who due to conflicts between his religious beliefs and the typical rock and roll band lifestyle. "when Randy Backman of the Guests Who became a Mormon in 1966, it led to tension in the band centering on differences between the stereotypical rock and roll band lifestyle and how that conflicted with Backman's religious beliefs."

podcast.title: "Heavy Metal Robots" Description (1970)
podcast.body: In the February 7, 1970, edition of Cream Magazine, music critic Lester Bangs described The Guess Who as "heavy metal robots" following their hit single "Undun." While this marked an early reference to music using the term "heavy metal," it was intended as an insult rather than a genre classification. "They're quite refreshing in the wake of all the heavy metal robots of the year past."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Bryce Decker's Rhythm Guitar Role
podcast.body: After his brief time with The Devarons, Bryce Decker, famous for his youthful attempt to board The Beatles' plane, had a second brief musical engagement playing rhythm guitar with the legendary band The Guess Who. "followed by a second brief moment on rhythm guitar with the legendary band The Guess Who."

podcast.title: Canadian Export Success
podcast.body: The Guess Who are mentioned among the earlier Canadian artists whose work contributed to the nation's music export growth. "Alannus Morse at Sarah McLaughlin, Celine Dion, Shania Twain, Rush, the Guests Who, and dozens and dozens and dozens of others."

podcast.title: Cancon Boosted Success (1970s)
podcast.body: The Guess Who were among the numerous Canadian rock bands whose careers were propelled by the Cancon rules in the 1970s, enabling them to become Canadian success stories. "Just on the rock side, we had Rush, April Wine, the Guess Who, Triumph, Crobar, Teenage Head, Max Webster, Chilowac, FM, Saga, and a foot-and-cold water."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Early Instability and Southern Ontario Shift
podcast.body: The Guess Who experienced several name and member changes early in their career before settling in Southern Ontario, where they would eventually achieve music history with a hard rock hit. "The band saw a few name changes and a few changes in members before they found themselves somewhere in Southern Ontario and about to make music history with a hard rocking hit."

podcast.title: Increased FM Airplay
podcast.body: Due to new FM radio rules in Canada that mandated playing more album tracks and Canadian content, The Guess Who's music, alongside others like Bachman-Turner Overdrive and Neil Young, saw significantly more airplay. This was in part because there weren't enough new Canadian bands of a certain caliber yet. "a lot more guest who, back then turn or overdrive the band and Neil Young got played."

podcast.title: Label's Preference for Ballads
podcast.body: The Guess Who's record label expressed a preference for ballads, specifically seeking another song in the vein of "These Eyes," despite the band's inclination towards hard rock. "Their label wanted something like the song These Eyes, they wanted another ballad."

podcast.title: Name Change Due to Stunt
podcast.body: The band, originally known as Chad Allen and the Expressions, was forced to change their name to The Guess Who after a publicity stunt by Quality Records. The label sent out a single with "Guess Who?" on it, leading DJs to mistakenly promote them as a hot new British invasion band when their cover of "Shake It All Over" became a hit. "the group had no choice but to change their name from Chad Allen and the expressions to the Guess Who."

podcast.title: Pre-Cancon Limited Impact
podcast.body: Before the implementation of Cancon, groups like The Guess Who could "make sort of a living by playing in front of 100 people on tours of North and Saskatchewan," but their impact on the world stage on behalf of Canada was minimal. "Okay, sure groups like the Guess Who could make sort of a living by playing in front of 100 people on tours of North and Saskatchewan, but that really didn't make much of an impact on behalf of Canada on the world stage."

podcast.title: Produced by Jack Richardson
podcast.body: The "best records" of The Guess Who were produced by the legendary Canadian producer Jack Richardson. "Jack did all the guess who's best records."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Producer During Glory Years
podcast.body: Jack Richardson served as the producer for The Guess Who during their most successful period, referred to as their "glory years." "In the late 60s, he got into the music industry and was the guest who was producer during their glory years."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: White House Performance Myth
podcast.body: It is a myth that The Guess Who were asked not to play "American Woman" when invited to perform at the White House by Richard Nixon. Although the band received criticism for playing there, their PR manager fabricated the story that Nixon requested them not to play the song, believing it would generate positive publicity. "not true that they were asked to not play American woman at the White House when Richard Nixon invited the band to play there. They did get a lot of crap for playing the White House and their PR manager said that it would be good publicity for them to say that Nixon said, hey, don't play that American woman song, but that did not happen."

xref.title: Early Career and Mentorship
xref.body: In the 1960s, Bob Ezrin secured a job at a recording studio with Jack Richardson, the producer for The Guess Who. He furthered his education by taking a summer course in music production taught by the legendary producer Phil Ramone. "In the 1960s, Bob got a job working in a recording studio with Jack Richardson, the guest who's producer. He also took a summer course in music production taught by the legendary producer Phil and Ramone."

xref.body: Jack Richardson is recognized as a legendary Canadian producer who was responsible for producing "all the guess who's best records." He is also the father of Garth Richardson, who produced Rage Against The Machine's debut album. "Jack did all the guess who's best records."

xref.title: Producer of Rage Against The Machine
xref.body: Garth Richardson is credited with producing Rage Against The Machine's debut record, contributing to its acclaimed audio quality. He is the son of Jack Richardson, a legendary Canadian producer known for his work on The Guess Who's most successful albums. "Props to Garth Richardson, the son of legendary Canadian producer Jack Richardson."
